best_for: Windows admins who need a light SSH, Telnet or serial client with saved sessions, plus command-line copy tools that work in scripts.
description:
PuTTY is a free client for SSH, the protocol most people use to log in to a remote server. It also speaks older protocols such as Telnet, Rlogin and SUPDUP. Simon Tatham started it and still writes most of the code, with a small team that answers mail, runs the nightly builds and keeps the wish list.

In plain terms: PuTTY opens a window, and whatever you type goes to the remote machine, while its replies show up in that window. You can change settings mid-session, such as port forwardings, from a menu instead of a key combination. Lines that PuTTY prints itself carry a small PuTTY icon, so a server cannot fake a login prompt. You can also make a Windows shortcut that opens one saved session directly.

points.title: More than one program
points.text: The installer brings PuTTY itself plus PSCP and PSFTP for file copy, Plink for scripts, Pageant as a key agent, and PuTTYgen for making keys. It is free under the MIT license.

points.title: It will not save passwords
points.text: PuTTY deliberately does not remember passwords. The FAQ points you to public key login instead, with keys made in PuTTYgen and held by Pageant.

points.title: Settings live in the registry
points.text: On Windows, saved sessions and host keys go in the registry under your user, not in a file. On a shared PC, run `putty -cleanup` before you leave or uninstall, because the uninstaller does not remove them.

points.title: No Mac version
points.text: There is no macOS build, and the FAQ says the team doubts it will finish one.

points.title: Pick 64-bit unless the PC is old
points.text: MSI installers exist for 64-bit x86, Arm64 and 32-bit x86; the 32-bit build is only for very old PCs. Single .exe files and zip packages are offered too, and the Microsoft Store carries the installers a few days after release.

points.title: Linux and pterm
points.text: On Linux, PuTTY is a Unix port that also includes pterm, a local terminal. The Flatpak listed here is a Flathub build that is not marked verified. The Windows listing keeps 12 versions; Linux lists only the current release.

points.title: You may not need it
points.text: Windows now includes OpenSSH, and the FAQ says plainly that is a fine choice. PuTTY still adds GUI session settings, logging options and serial port support.
